```{r}
#| label: neighborhood-data
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(scales)
library(plotly)

nbhd_agg <- read.csv("../data/canarsie-neighborhoods.csv")
nbhd_agg$cluster <- factor(nbhd_agg$cluster)
MY_NEIGHBORHOOD <- "CANARSIE"
my_row <- filter(nbhd_agg, NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME == MY_NEIGHBORHOOD)
cluster_names <- c("1" = "Budget basics", "2" = "Mid-market", "3" = "Luxury")
nbhd_agg <- nbhd_agg %>% mutate(
  hover = paste0(NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME,
    "<br>Sales: ", comma(total_sales),
    "<br>Median $/sq ft: ", dollar(median_psf),
    "<br>Median sale price: ", dollar(median_price),
    "<br>Cluster ", cluster, ": ", cluster_names[as.character(cluster)])
)
```

## The approach

I combined NYC sales data with neighborhood clustering, local pricing models, quarterly forecasting, and financial scenario analysis in R.

**Methods:** Clustering · Regression · ETS · NPV

## What I found

- **Focus on the core.** Standard properties represented 48.3% of the clustered sample, offering the largest initial listing pool.
- **Use local context.** A citywide model overpredicted Canarsie prices. Local pricing and neighborhood knowledge matter.
- **Enter lean.** The assignment model favored a 4.3% commission and no salaried staff. Returns turned negative in the conservative scenario.

### Strategic Clustering — All NYC Neighborhoods

```{r}
#| label: strategic-clustering
#| fig-alt: "Interactive scatter plot of 256 NYC neighborhoods by residential sales count and median price per square foot. Canarsie is marked by a black diamond."

p <- ggplot(nbhd_agg, aes(x = total_sales, y = median_psf, color = cluster, text = hover)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = filter(nbhd_agg, NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME == MY_NEIGHBORHOOD),
             color = "black", size = 5, shape = 18) +
  geom_text(data = filter(nbhd_agg, NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME == MY_NEIGHBORHOOD),
            aes(label = NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME), vjust = -1, color = "black", size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1" = "#638f9b", "2" = "#17685f", "3" = "#bb7953"),
                     labels = c("1 · Budget basics", "2 · Mid-market", "3 · Luxury")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Strategic Clustering — All NYC Neighborhoods",
       subtitle = "Diamond = Canarsie",
       x = "Total Sales Since 2009", y = "Median $/Sq Ft", color = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 16, color = "#223343"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#586570"))

chart <- ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text", height = 500)
for (i in seq_along(chart$x$data)) {
  if (identical(chart$x$data[[i]]$mode, "text")) {
    chart$x$data[[i]]$textposition <- "top center"
    chart$x$data[[i]]$hoverinfo <- "skip"
  }
  name <- chart$x$data[[i]]$name
  if (!is.null(name) && name %in% names(cluster_names)) {
    chart$x$data[[i]]$name <- paste(name, cluster_names[name], sep = " · ")
  }
}
chart %>%
  layout(title = list(text = ""), legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.22),
         margin = list(t = 15, b = 110, l = 65, r = 20),
         paper_bgcolor = "#fbfaf7", plot_bgcolor = "#fbfaf7",
         font = list(family = "Avenir Next, Segoe UI, Arial", color = "#223343"),
         hoverlabel = list(bgcolor = "#223343", font = list(color = "white"))) %>%
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, scrollZoom = FALSE,
         modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("lasso2d", "select2d"))
```

### What this means for Canarsie

Canarsie belongs to **Cluster 2: Mid-market**, the notebook's higher-volume group. Its **5,955 sales** and **$268.40 median price per square foot** point to an established residential market at a lower price per square foot than the cluster average of about **$337**.

The luxury cluster sits much higher on the price axis, while many mid-market neighborhoods sit farther to the right. For market entry, the chart helps separate transaction activity from pricing and identify comparable neighborhoods.

### Closest pricing peers

These five neighborhoods share Canarsie's cluster and have the closest median prices per square foot. They provide useful comparison markets, rather than a claim that every property is equivalent.

```{r}
#| label: neighborhood-peers
peers <- nbhd_agg %>%
  filter(cluster == my_row$cluster, NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME != MY_NEIGHBORHOOD) %>%
  arrange(abs(median_psf - my_row$median_psf)) %>%
  head(5) %>%
  transmute(Neighborhood = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(NEIGHBORHOOD_NAME)),
            Sales = comma(total_sales),
            `Median $/sq ft` = dollar(median_psf),
            `Median sale price` = dollar(median_price))
knitr::kable(peers, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

### How the clusters were built

The analysis keeps residential sales with a positive price and known, positive gross square footage. Neighborhoods need at least two qualifying sales. K-means groups them using four standardized measures: median sale price, transaction count, median price per square foot, and sale-price variability (**k = 3; seed = 42**).

This chart shows two of those four measures. Sales counts describe the cleaned sample; cluster names are descriptive labels from the analysis. Historical clusters are not forecasts of future prices.

*Academic findings under assignment assumptions. Samples differ by analytical stage.*
